chunks: As for what Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā narrated from al-ʿAmrakī, from ʿAlī ibn Jaʿfar, from his brother Mūsā ibn Jaʿfar عليه السلام, he said:

I asked him about a man who has a wart or a wound: is it permissible for him to cut off the wart while he is in his salat (prayer), or to pluck some flesh from that wound and lance it? He said: If he does not fear that blood will flow, then there is no problem; but if he fears that blood will flow, then he should not do it.

And about a man who is in his salat (prayer), then another man throws something at him and wounds his head, so blood flows. He turns away, washes it, and does not speak until he returns to the mosque. Should he count what he has already prayed, or should he begin the salat (prayer) anew? He said: He should begin the salat (prayer) anew and not count anything of what he had prayed.

So the proper way regarding this report is that we interpret it as referring to one who turned around until he faced away from the qiblah, for that invalidates his salat (prayer). It is also possible that it was issued in the context of taqiyyah, because according to many of the ʿAmmah, the خروج of blood nullifies wudu (ablution), and when wudu (ablution) is nullified, it necessitates repeating the salat (prayer) from its beginning, as we have mentioned before.

key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation for protection in a context of opposing legal views
key_terms.الْمَسْجِدِ: the mosque to which the person returned
key_terms.صَلَاتِهِ: his salat (prayer), the ritual prayer being performed

ai.seo_question: Does bleeding or treating a wound during salat (prayer) invalidate the prayer in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses rulings related to salat (prayer) when a person has a wart or wound, and whether minor bodily actions during prayer are permissible. It also addresses a case of bleeding during prayer and presents the scholarly reconciliation that the prayer must be restarted if one turned away from the qiblah, or that the report may have been stated in taqiyyah due to the view of many among the ʿAmmah that blood nullifies wudu (ablution).
